item.title: EnvHarness: Awakening Static Worlds for Agent Learning
item.description: By Chengsong Huang, Zifeng Wang, Rujun Han (Washington University in St. Louis; Google Cloud AI Research; Google Cloud; University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill) EnvHarness: Awakening Static Worlds for Agent Learning, by Chengsong Huang, Zifeng Wang, and Rujun Han, with fourteen more authors including Burak Gokturk, Tomas Pfister, and Chen-Yu Lee. Huang did this work while interning at Google Cloud AI Research, and the affiliation list covers Washington University in St. Louis, Google Cloud AI Research, Google Cloud, and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Here is the premise, and it is a reasonable one. As language models become agents, the scarce resource for training shifts from curated text data to interactive environments. Those environments are hand-built: someone hardcodes interaction logic and a verifier, and the result behaves identically whether it faces a novice or a competent policy. Two failure modes follow. A static environment cannot target the specific weaknesses of the policy you actually have, and once the policy learns to solve its existing tasks, the environment has nothing left to teach. Automated environment generation exists as an alternative, with systems like GenEnv simulating environments and their feedback inside a model, VeriEnv synthesizing executable environments programmatically, and SWE-smith generating new task instances within an existing benchmark. But those pipelines are domain-specific, each built separately for web navigation, programming, or tool use, and because both tasks and verifiers come out of a model, teams over-generate and filter heavily without ever guaranteeing correctness. EnvHarness takes a different position: stop authoring new environments, and reshape the ones you already trust.

item.title: FACET: Preserving Source Intent and Executable State in Terminal Task Synthesis
item.description: By Kou Shi, Zun Wang, Qisheng Su (MoE Key Lab of BIPC, University of Science and Technology of China; Shanghai AI Laboratory; Fudan University) FACET: Preserving Source Intent and Executable State in Terminal Task Synthesis, by Kou Shi, Zun Wang, and Qisheng Su, with ten more authors including Feng Zhao as corresponding author. The affiliations are the MoE Key Lab of BIPC at the University of Science and Technology of China, Shanghai AI Laboratory, and Fudan University. The problem this paper attacks is concrete: training terminal agents needs scalable, executable supervision, and every synthesized terminal task is a tightly coupled bundle of an instruction, an initialized environment, a reference solution, and an executable verifier, packaged in the Harbor format that Terminal-Bench uses. If those artifacts are generated under inconsistent assumptions you get tasks that cannot be solved or that grade incorrectly. Two failure mechanisms dominate multi-stage synthesis pipelines. First, information loss: source material rich in capabilities, dependencies, intermediate states, input-output contracts, and procedural constraints gets progressively compressed into a simplified task description, preserving only a fraction of the available structure. Second, artifact drift: an instruction references a file never realized in the environment, a solution assumes a different schema or dependency version, or a verifier tests a state the generated task cannot produce. Passing textual specifications between generation stages mitigates neither problem, because text is not a shared realized state.

item.title: SWE-bench Science: Can Coding Agents Resolve Engineering Tasks in Science?
item.description: By Zhipeng Xu, Jiahao Lu, Yining Zheng (Shanghai Innovation Institute; Fudan University) SWE-bench Science: Can Coding Agents Resolve Engineering Tasks in Science?, by Zhipeng Xu, Jiahao Lu, and Yining Zheng, with Yuxin Wang and Xipeng Qiu as corresponding authors, all affiliated with the Shanghai Innovation Institute and Fudan University. The motivation is worth stating carefully because this is not benchmark inflation. Software now functions as part of the scientific instrument itself: simulations, instrument processing pipelines, surrogate models, candidate search in chemistry and biology, reproduction of published results. A defective patch to that software corrupts not just a program but the evidence behind a scientific conclusion. Existing coding-agent evaluations mostly report aggregate task success, which cannot tell you why an agent failed on scientific code. This paper contributes a repository-level benchmark of 119 tasks drawn from 98 unique GitHub repositories across 20 scientific domains, plus a failure-mode taxonomy and a paired ablation on scientific knowledge. Code and data are public through GitHub and Hugging Face under the OpenMOSS organization, with a leaderboard maintained separately. Scale first. Input repositories average about 80,600 non-empty lines, ranging from 174 to over two million. Reference patches add an average of 117.81 lines and delete 44.53. Chemistry is the largest domain at 24 tasks, then materials science with 16, biology with 13, biomedical engineering with 12, physics with 11; six domains contribute a single task each. Tasks fall into three paradigms: Issue-driven at 52 tasks, repairing known historical defects under low distortion; Expert-exploratory at 49, where the agent must autonomously find an unknown root cause from an observed anomaly such as abnormal convergence or biased results, with any underlying issue used only as

item.title: Repo0: Design-Driven Zero-to-All Code Generation
item.description: By Silin Chen, Haoyi Teng, Xiaodong Gu (Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Chongqing University) Repo0: Design-Driven Zero-to-All Code Generation, by Silin Chen and Haoyi Teng as equal first authors, Xiaodong Gu as corresponding author, with Yuling Shi, Jiale Huang, Yongpan Wang, Hongyu Zhang, and Haibing Guan. The affiliations are Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Chongqing University. The setting is zero-to-all code generation: an agent receives natural-language requirements and must construct an entire software project from nothing while maintaining a modular repository architecture throughout. Most existing systems quietly assume the opposite, that component boundaries, package organization, and dependency graphs are already given, which is why repository-completion work looks so much better than it should. The authors' diagnosis of prior systems, including RPG, the strongest graph-based baseline, is that they treat software design as a static artifact: a perfect architectural blueprint generated in one initial planning stage, then rigidly executed. Anyone who has shipped software knows the blueprint is wrong by the time implementation starts; generated code reveals whether planned components were ever cohesive or whether dependency edges are entangled. Repo0's answer is continuous structural evolution around an explicit architectural state, instantiated as what they call a Dual-DAG. Two directed acyclic graphs plus an alignment relation. The requirement-level DAG holds high-level requirements decomposed into sub-requirements, and its edges encode functional coordination: two requirements logically used together and needing joint consideration for behavior, inputs, and outputs. item.title: FlashPrefill V2: Block-Sparse Prefill Attention for Long-Context LLM Serving
item.description: By Qihang Fan, Huaibo Huang, Zhiying Wu (MAIS and NLPR, CASIA; UCAS; WeChat, Tencent) FlashPrefill V2: Block-Sparse Prefill Attention for Long-Context LLM Serving, by Qihang Fan, Huaibo Huang, and Zhiying Wu, with Bingning Wang as project leader and Ran He. The affiliations are the Institute of Automation of the Chinese Academy of Sciences through its MAIS and NLPR labs, the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, and WeChat at Tencent; the first author completed the work during an internship at WeChat. Context for the audience: attention cost during prefill grows with the square of sequence length, and every training-free sparse-attention method lives or dies on three practical questions. Does accuracy survive aggressive sparsity? Is the kernel competitive with current dense implementations rather than last generation's? And does it work inside a real serving stack with paged KV cache and continuous batching? Their previous FlashPrefill answered none of those fully. It discovered patterns instantaneously using mean-pooled keys and max-based dynamic thresholding, avoiding the global sorting that Top-k selection requires, but accuracy degraded without bound under extreme sparsity, the kernel was built on FlashAttention-2's execution model, which leaves Hopper tensor-core throughput on the table, and it assumed a contiguous KV layout incompatible with any modern serving framework. V2 addresses exactly these three gaps.

item.title: FlowEvo: Self-Evolving Agents through the Co-Evolution of Workflows and Executable Skills
item.description: By Zeyu Ren, Ling Yue, Ran Li (Southeast University; Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute; The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology) FlowEvo: Self-Evolving Agents through the Co-Evolution of Workflows and Executable Skills, by Zeyu Ren, Ling Yue, and Ran Li, with Yishu Wang, Shengxiang Xu, Hanmo Liu, Shaowu Pan, and Shimin Di. The affiliations are Southeast University, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, and the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. The gap this paper identifies is real and worth articulating precisely. Workflow-based agents construct procedures at inference time: decomposition, tool calls, code generation, checking, repair. But whatever structure a successful episode discovers gets discarded when the episode ends. Skill libraries preserve reusable routines as executable objects, yet they are typically assembled offline for a fixed task distribution rather than growing from the agent's own problem solving. Text memories such as Agent Workflow Memory sit in between: they describe what worked but cannot be invoked or validated, so reuse still depends on the model re-deriving the procedure from prose. FlowEvo is a training-free framework that closes this loop: successful workflows are compiled into callable skill records stored in a persistent bank, and those skills feed back into later workflow construction either through direct execution or as structured context. Model weights never change.

item.title: Self-Supervised Visual On-Policy Distillation
item.description: By Yijiang Li, Yijun Liang, Yunjie Tian (UC San Diego; University of Maryland, College Park; Georgia Institute of Technology; Johns Hopkins University; University of Oxford) Self-Supervised Visual On-Policy Distillation, by Yijiang Li of UC San Diego, Yijun Liang of the University of Maryland, College Park, and Yunjie Tian, an independent researcher, with co-authors from Georgia Institute of Technology, Johns Hopkins University, and the University of Oxford. On-policy distillation works because the teacher knows something the student does not: either it is a bigger model, or someone hands it privileged material such as reference answers or ground-truth regions of interest. This paper asks where the asymmetry comes from when you have none of that, and the answer is refreshingly blunt: take information away from the student instead of giving it to the teacher. Train the student on degraded views of the image while an exponential-moving-average copy of itself scores the same prefixes under the clean image. No annotations, no rewards, no second model. Whether that trick survives contact with real benchmarks is the question, so let us look at the numbers rather than the framing. The method, called S2VOPD, is deliberately thin. For each image-question pair, the student samples its own rollouts conditioned on a transformed view, x-tilde equals T of x, while an EMA teacher re-evaluates every visited prefix using the original clean image. The training objective minimizes a per-token divergence between the teacher distribution given the clean view and the student distribution given the corrupted view, averaged along trajectories the student generated itself, which keeps supervision on exactly the prefixes the student visits at inference time. item.title: Beyond Final Scores: A Systematic Evaluation of Agents for Long-Horizon AI Research and Development
item.description: By Yiwei Li, Wanli Yang, Hexiang Tan (Meituan; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences) Beyond Final Scores: A Systematic Evaluation of Agents for Long-Horizon AI Research and Development, by Yiwei Li, Wanli Yang, and Hexiang Tan, from Meituan and the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences. The premise is that the field evaluates research agents the wrong way. Agents run long closed-loop cycles of proposing changes, executing experiments, reading verifier feedback, and revising, but benchmarks score them on one final number, which hides where progress was gained, where it leaked away, whether accumulated experience helps or hurts later decisions, and whether the harness rather than the model is doing the work. This report decomposes the loop into rule-based process metrics, runs controlled experience-ablation experiments, varies the agent harness, and then asks an LLM judge with human review whether any solution is actually novel. Seven frontier models, thirty-six tasks, three rollouts each, roughly one hundred thousand U.S. dollars in inference spend. That budget buys credibility; read on for what it bought. The setup first. Tasks come from AutoLab in four families: Model Development with seven tasks, System Optimization with fifteen, Puzzle and Challenge with ten, and CUDA with four. Each task ships a correct but deliberately suboptimal starting artifact, an expert reference solution, a wall-clock budget between two and twelve hours, and an automated verifier scoring zero to one against that scale. Seven models were evaluated: Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GLM 5.2, Kimi K2.7-Code, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and LongCat-2.0. The main comparison holds Claude Code version 2.1.152 fixed as a shared harness across all models; native harnesses and OpenCode enter only in a dedicated ablation. Three independent rollouts per model-task pair yield seven hundred fifty-s

item.title: SimpleOPD: Simple Tokenizer-Agnostic On-Policy Distillation for Long-Context Reasoning
item.description: By Haonan He, Haodi Lei, Yun Luo (Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory) SimpleOPD: Simple Tokenizer-Agnostic On-Policy Distillation for Long-Context Reasoning, by Haonan He, Haodi Lei, and Yun Luo, with the SU-01 Team at Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. The problem is specific and practical. On-policy distillation is now a standard post-training tool: the student generates its own trajectories, and a teacher provides dense token-level supervision on exactly the states the student visits. But nearly all published work assumes teacher and student share a vocabulary. Try distilling from a long-context reasoning teacher that writes hundred-thousand-token proofs into a short-context student from a different model family, and three things break: the tokenizers do not align, the teacher prefers responses longer than the student's context budget, and training destabilizes into length explosion, truncation, and repetition loops. This paper reports what actually breaks when you attempt this transfer and two small fixes that make it work. The results are strong enough to matter; the mechanism is simple enough to ship. The cross-tokenizer alignment first, because it is the load-bearing idea. Rather than mapping one vocabulary onto another, SimpleOPD performs distillation in shared text space. The student generates a response under its own tokenizer and chat template. That response string is appended to the context reconstructed under the teacher's own chat template, and the teacher tokenizes it natively. Then a linear two-pointer scan walks both tokenizations of the identical response string: whenever the accumulated text prefixes match and the current tokens contribute the exact same text span, the pair is aligned and inherits supervision; partially overlapping spans are skipped entirely, because you cannot uniquely assign one teacher log-probability across mu

item.title: Intern-S2-Mobius: Foundation Model with Decoupled Knowledge and Reasoning
item.description: By Kai Chen, Jifeng Ding, Ning Ding (Shanghai AI Laboratory) Intern-S2-Mobius: Foundation Model with Decoupled Knowledge and Reasoning, by Kai Chen, Jifeng Ding, and Ning Ding, with the Intern-S2-Mobius Team at the Shanghai AI Laboratory. The claim is architectural and blunt: binding knowledge storage, the feed-forward network, to reasoning operators, self-attention, layer by layer inside every Transformer block wastes both compute and parameters. Mobius-v0 cuts that binding. One globally shared Memory, built from feed-forward parameters, stores knowledge vectors; multiple Reasoner layers, built from self-attention, iteratively query it through their hidden states. Every reasoning layer reads the entire knowledge repository rather than only what the previous layer passed down. The paper reports a seven-billion-parameter model trained from scratch matching a Transformer baseline's downstream score using sixty-two point six percent of the training data, and a thirty-five-billion production model converted from Qwen3.5 delivering nearly four times end-to-end inference speedup at comparable quality. Those are strong claims for an architecture paper, so the details deserve scrutiny. Two design choices do the work. First, backward residual connection. Standard residuals are unidirectional: shallow states can be read by deep layers, but deep-layer attention processes only knowledge originating from shallow layers. If critical knowledge fails to activate early, the model compensates by generating low-information tokens in an explicit chain of thought and trying again next forward pass. A direct bidirectional residual is infrastructure-hostile, so Mobius gets the effect indirectly: since all Reasoners share one memory, every layer accesses everything, which functions as a backward path. item.title: Latent On-Policy Self-Distillation
item.description: By Guibin Zhang, Jiayang Lyu, Ran Sun (National University of Singapore; Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications; Shanghai Jiao Tong University) Latent On-Policy Self-Distillation, by Guibin Zhang of the National University of Singapore, Jiayang Lyu of Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, and Ran Sun, with co-authors from Shanghai Jiao Tong University. The paper addresses the central design question in self-evolving agents: when a model teaches itself from experience, what should the teacher be allowed to see? On-policy self-distillation answers this today with designer-specified artifacts. The teacher gets verified reasoning traces, or final answers, or environment feedback, or successful sibling rollouts, or retrieved documents, and each variant works somewhere and fails somewhere else. LOPD's move is structural rather than incremental: stop hand-designing the privilege entirely. Compose retrieved raw trajectories into continuous latent tokens, make that composition learnable end-to-end alongside the student, and let gradient descent decide what experience is worth encoding for supervision. After training you throw away everything except the student. The mechanics, concretely. An experience bank stores successful rollouts offline as task descriptions plus compact action-result traces with verbose observations stripped. At training time a dense retriever fetches entries by cosine similarity over task-trace pairs, defaulting to three. A composer then processes each retrieved item: an encoder with trainable LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone maps the task-experience pair into hidden states, and a QFormer-style cross-attention compressor with learned queries squeezes variable-length states into exactly thirty-two continuous latent tokens per experience, ninety-six tokens total. item.title: Spark-to-Paper: End-to-End Research Paper Generation as a Composable Skill
item.description: By Zhuoyang Qian, Biao Wu, Yiran Wang (Vast Intelligence Lab; University of Technology Sydney) Spark-to-Paper: End-to-End Research Paper Generation as a Composable Skill, by Zhuoyang Qian, Biao Wu, and Yiran Wang, from the Vast Intelligence Lab and the University of Technology Sydney. The premise: an entire research pipeline, literature retrieval through experiments, figures, and a compiled manuscript, implemented as thirteen composable skills inside an ordinary coding assistant, with no orchestration server, no graph database, and no separate agent platform. For teams already living inside tools like Claude Code, that deployment story matters more than any benchmark delta, so let us take the system apart. The gap the authors claim is real enough. Standalone autonomous-research systems such as AI Scientist, AI Scientist-v2, Agent Laboratory, and Kosmos match or exceed the pipeline breadth but ship as dedicated codebases with their own infrastructure, sometimes a graph database or cluster scheduler on top. Lightweight skill-based writing assistants stay inside the coding assistant but neither run real experiments end to end nor produce editable vector figures rather than embedded bitmaps, the two capabilities at the center of this paper. The closest prior analogue pairs an automated researcher with an automated reviewer trained to critique it, but still stops short of executing experiments. Spark-to-Paper positions itself between those poles, and to its credit the paper marks its own comparison table and breadth chart as ordinal assessments derived from each compared system's public documentation rather than measurements. Keep that caveat in mind whenever the positioning figure comes up.

item.title: OpenART: Scaling Agent Red Teaming via Open-Ended Environment Evolution
item.description: By Yunhao Chen, Xin Wang, Yixu Wang (Fudan University; Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory; XSafeAI) OpenART: Scaling Agent Red Teaming via Open-Ended Environment Evolution, by Yunhao Chen, Xin Wang, and Yixu Wang, from Fudan University, the Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, and XSafeAI. The core reframing: stop treating a prompt as the unit of red teaming and treat the persistent executable environment as the unit instead. The task objective and safety contract stay fixed while only the target-visible state evolves across rounds. If you ship coding agents against real workspaces, the headline finding should get your attention: pooled strict attack success of 85 percent across 75 agent-model configurations, with environment evolution gaining almost nothing on simple tasks but up to 17.6 points on the most complex ones. First, scale, because that is what separates this from prior agent-safety benchmarks. Over 10,000 validated stateful scenarios spanning 50 domains organized into eight groups, from software and IT data with 13 domains down to digital work and knowledge with 3, grounded in real capability surfaces such as Jira, Slack, GitHub, Gmail, Salesforce, Notion, Figma, Grafana, and dbt. The scenario corpus draws on more than 500,000 tools, MCPs, and skills collected following SkillNet. Median workload is 97 tool calls per scenario with an interquartile range of 90 to 100, dependency depth 32, parallel width 12.5, 96.5 state objects, and 7.5 persistent file formats per task, against 1 to 15 tool calls for InjeAgent, AgentDojo, AgentHarm, ASB, ToolEmu, and DTap, none of which persist state across file formats at all. The same validated scenario projects through adapters into 15 deployed agent runtimes, including Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Aider, Goose, Copilot CLI, Continue CLI, Kilo, Nanobot, Oh My Pi, OpenClaw, Pi, CodeWhale, Qwen Code, and H

item.title: AI4AI at Test-Time: Strong-to-Weak Capability Transfer via Harnesses
item.description: By Cheng Qian, Wenting Zhao, Liangwei Yang (Salesforce AI Research; University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) AI4AI at Test-Time: Strong-to-Weak Capability Transfer via Harnesses, by Cheng Qian, Wenting Zhao, and Liangwei Yang, from Salesforce AI Research and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. The question is clean: can a strong builder model write inference-time scaffolding that lifts a weak target model without touching a single parameter? The answer across 72 controlled runs is yes, dramatically. GPT-5.4-mini's macro accuracy on four Theory-of-Mind benchmarks goes from 0.488 to a best of 0.912, and the mechanism analysis tells you exactly where the gains come from, which is what makes this paper useful rather than just another leaderboard entry. Setup first, because the protocol is what makes the result credible. Four benchmarks aggregate into a hidden test set of 3,900 items: BigToM with 1,200 binary belief, goal, and action questions hinging on whether an agent observed a world change, procedurally generated from causal templates; Hi-ToM with 1,200 nested belief questions across recursion orders zero through four with deception and multi-room object tracking; MMToM-QA with 600 binary Bayesian goal and belief inference items from action traces in household settings; MuMA-ToM with 900 three-choice questions over goals, beliefs, and beliefs about others' goals in embodied multi-agent interactions. Only text-format questions are used. Each builder gets only a 195-item validation slice, 5 percent drawn by fixed seed, plus a rule file describing task instructions and submission format and a demonstration file showing how to call the target. item.title: Mechanist: AI as a Scientific Instrument for Discovering the Mechanisms of Intelligence
item.description: By Mengru Wang, Junfeng Fang, Shuofei Qiao (Zhejiang University; National University of Singapore; Southern University of Science and Technology) Mechanist: AI as a Scientific Instrument for Discovering the Mechanisms of Intelligence, by Mengru Wang, Junfeng Fang, and Shuofei Qiao, from Zhejiang University, the National University of Singapore, the Southern University of Science and Technology, Heriot-Watt University, UC San Diego, and Northeastern University. The framing is ambitious but concrete: instead of an AI scientist that does science in some generic domain, build an agentic system specialized to one science, mechanistic interpretability, and measure whether it can autonomously discover, verify, and exploit mechanisms inside models. Three case results anchor it: a cross-modal subliminal learning risk, a causal theory of belief-state heads, and mechanism-guided steering of a DNA foundation model. The infrastructure is the first real contribution. An interpretability-focused knowledge graph of roughly 13,000 papers plus research blogs, built on an OpenAlex-derived corpus, organized along three axes: object of study, application scenario, and analysis method. In its current form it holds about 13,900 interpretability papers, over 107,000 nodes, and roughly 1.86 million edges. DeepSeek-V3.2-Thinking extracted attributes with unsupported or ambiguous items deliberately left unspecified rather than inferred. Quality control used Claude Opus 4.7 as an LLM judge plus three human annotators auditing 100 sampled records, yielding accuracy above 90 percent, with disagreements feeding back into extraction prompts before reprocessing. This graph plugs into SciAtlas, a multidisciplinary database of more than 43 million papers across 26 fields. item.title: SkillZip: Contract-Preserving Graph Compression for Scalable Agent Skill Libraries
item.description: By Xingyu Tan, Xiaoyang Wang, Qing Liu (UNSW Sydney; CSIRO) SkillZip: Contract-Preserving Graph Compression for Scalable Agent Skill Libraries, by Xingyu Tan, Xiaoyang Wang, and Qing Liu, from UNSW Sydney and CSIRO. The problem will be familiar to anyone running a skill library at scale: skills are retrieved as whole packages, compressed as plain text, and turned into execution graphs only after retrieval, and that unit mismatch is exactly where things fail. Whole-skill exposure wastes context on irrelevant sections, text summarization can silently drop a precondition or a verifier hook, and task-time graph compilation never improves the library itself. SkillZip's answer is to make the section-level procedural graph the persistent storage format, then compress it in a way that provably keeps procedures executable. The representation comes first. Each skill package is decomposed by Sec2Graph into typed section nodes with nine execution roles: Intent, Trigger, Input, Precondition, Operation, Resource, Failure, Verifier, Output. Segmentation uses headings, lists, code blocks, warnings, argument descriptions, tool references, and tests as boundary cues, with a model-assisted parser refining when cues run out, always preserving source pointers back to the original text; role assignment is semantic, so in a tabular skill infer-the-delimiter is an Operation while verify-row-counts-unchanged is a Verifier regardless of file position. Each node carries input-output signatures, resources, guard and verifier conditions, and provenance. Edges come in four kinds: typed dependencies such as requires, binds, uses-resource, verifies, and repairs; weak-order edges for local sequence inside a skill; skill-membership edges; and equivalence links connecting compatible occurrences to shared canonical prototypes that expose cross-skill reuse, like tabular ingestion shared by cleaning, pivo

item.title: Can LLM Agents Stick to the Script? A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Consistency in Interactive Narratives
item.description: By Yingpeng Ma, Jianhao Yan, Bei Shi (NLP2CT Lab, University of Macau; Westlake University; Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen; University of Cambridge; University of Aberdeen) Can LLM Agents Stick to the Script? A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Consistency in Interactive Narratives, by Yingpeng Ma, Jianhao Yan, and Bei Shi, from the NLP2CT Lab at the University of Macau, Westlake University, Harbin Institute of Technology Shenzhen, the University of Cambridge, and the University of Aberdeen. The task is Narrative Commitment Preservation: an agent narrating an interactive story must keep established facts fixed, honor ordering and invariant constraints, acknowledge player actions, and still advance the plot across a hundred turns. If that sounds soft, note the authors' own framing applies directly to coding agents, where a new request must not silently break implemented behavior, interface contracts, tests, or safety requirements. Same structure, different skin. The benchmark construction starts from the CMU Movie Summary Corpus. Human experts clean the candidate pool of duplicate records, mismatched characters, and incomplete synopses, then manually select 100 movies to maximize genre spread across 18 categories, action and science fiction leading at 13 and 12 percent, comedy 11, western 9, fantasy 8, crime 7. Each environment pairs a synopsis with a specific in-story character designated as the player role, not necessarily a protagonist, and every annotation obeys point-of-view discipline: only facts that character could plausibly observe or know at that point in the story, with explicit future-sight isolation on the initial state preventing omniscient leakage. Genre tags are manually annotated as primary plus secondary per movie.
